catalog_quote: [p. 19] Le mokilko distingue deux registres, haut (á) et bas (à). La combinaison de ces deux tons donne deux ton modulés: un, ton tombant haut-bas (a) et un ton montant bas-haut (ă). Ceux-ci peuvent être illustrés par les paires (ou triplets) minimales suivantes: choisir (subjon.) bèerè enquête: bèeré arbre sp.: béerè: máàyé cérémonie: máayè piéton wíiké kònsó appeler: wíikè fille se disperser vie. màayé vent bùrwé dêchet de: búrwè fronde boisson ... [p. 20] ... ton tombant ne se trouve qu'en position médiane. S'il apparaît en finale il s'agit en majeure partie soit d'un mot emprunté (arabe ou kenga en général), soit d'un mot ayant une origine onomatopéique/idéophonique. Parmi ces mots on trouve beaucoup de noms désignant des animaux (dans de contes), des insectes ... secondaire résulte de la combinaison d'un ton haut final et du ton bas du suffixe défini -n; par ex. kùlé 'homme', kùlé-n → kùlên 'l'homme'. Le ton montant bas-haut (a) ne résulte que d'une combinaison d'un ton bas final et d'un ton haut de l'élément ...

sweep_summary: Mukulu (muku1242) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Roberts 2000 'Accent clash in Mukulu verbs' (9-pp. WALC 22 Legon conference paper), is about accent in this language's verbs but is not obtainable: Glottolog's hh record shows Hammarstrom holds a private PDF; Crossref, Bing exact-title search and the live OLAC/SIL archive listing for [moz] are all negative; Its content is known only second-hand via Pearce 2006 (Phonology 23: 261-262, cited with full WALC 22 details), which lists Mukulu among Chadic languages 'described as pitch accent languages' with 'a limited selection of tone patterns in verbs' -- consistent with Hellmuth & Pearce 2020 (at most one H per word, per Pearce 2006) and with the earlier on-disk findings (Lukas 1977 declined to study Mukulu phonology/Druckakzent; Jungraithmayr 1990 gives a two-level tone system and no accent section). No source read states a stress-placement rule; Roberts 2000 remains high priority to acquire (ask Hammarstrom or SIL Chad / James Roberts directly). new_statements.quote: Les tons. Le mokilko distingue deux registres, haut (á) et bas (à). La combinaison de ces deux tons donne deux ton[s] modulés : un ton tombant haut-bas (â) et un ton montant bas-haut (ǎ). Ceux-ci peuvent être illustrés par les paires (ou triplets) minimales suivantes : choisir (subjon.) bèerè : enquête bèeré : arbre sp. béerè ... [p. 20] Le ton tombant ne se trouve qu'en position médiane. S'il apparaît en finale il s'agit en majeure partie soit d'un mot emprunté (arabe ou kenga en général), soit d'un mot ayant une origine onomatopéique/idéophonique ... [un] ton tombant secondaire résulte de la combinaison d'un ton haut final et du ton bas du suffixe défini -n ; par ex. kùlé 'homme', kùlé-n → kùlên 'l'homme'.
new_statements.translation: Tones. Mokilko distinguishes two registers, high (á) and low (à). The combination of these two tones yields two contour tones: a falling high-low (â) and a rising low-high (ǎ). These can be illustrated by the following minimal pairs (or triplets): 'choose' (subjunctive) bèerè : 'inquiry' bèeré : 'tree sp.' béerè ... The falling tone occurs only in medial position; if it appears finally the word is mostly either a loan (Arabic or Kenga) or of onomatopoeic/ideophonic origin ... a secondary falling tone results from the combination of a final high tone with the low tone of the definite suffix -n, e.g. kùlé 'man', kùlé-n > kùlên 'the man'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The reference description treats Mokilko as a two-level tone language (H, L, with derived HL and LH contours on single syllables, lexically and grammatically contrastive) and says nothing about word stress or accent; no placement rule for stress is given anywhere that could be opened. Lukas 1977 likewise marks three tones and explicitly declines to analyse phonology, noting only that a 'Druckakzent' exists (a future suffix carries it, with falling tone) and that Fédry's Dangaléat stress rules may be relevant. An accentual analysis exists only in unpublished SIL Chad work (Sharp 1997 ms; Roberts 2000 'Accent clash in Mukulu verbs').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tonal: falling tone word-final mostly in Arabic/Kenga loans and ideophones; Lukas: future suffix bears Druckakzent with falling tone.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical/grammatical tone in citation forms from a lexicon; statement seen only through Google Books snippets (the words 'accent', 'accentué', 'accentuation', 'intensité', 'intonation', 'prosodie' do not occur anywhere in the volume according to in-volume search). Variety: Mokilko proper as spoken at Mokoulou (Guéra), Jungraithmayr's fieldwork 1970s-80s.
new_statements.identity_note: Mokilko (Jungraithmayr's name, autonym-based; village Mokoulou) = Mukulu (Lukas 1977) = Gergiko/Guerguiko (SIL Chad orthography name) = Djonkor/Dyongor of Guéra; ISO moz, Glottolog muku1242, a single-language unit within East Chadic B (B2). Jungraithmayr 1990 and Lukas 1977 both describe the Mokilko proper dialect of Mokoulou village; other dialects (Seginki, Doliki, Moriko, Mezimko, Gugiko) undescribed. Not to be confused with Migaama ('Djonkor of Abou Telfane').

new_statements.quote: Other Chadic languages have been described as pitch-accent languages, including Masa (Barreteau 1995, De Dominicis 2003), where the patterns are largely predictable from the grammatical category and the voicing of the initial obstruent, Mofu (Barreteau 1995), with four melodies on the verbs, LLL, HLL, LHL and LLH, and Mukulu (Roberts 2000), which also has a limited selection of tone patterns in verbs.

new_statements.reading: Not a first-hand stress statement: Pearce reports that Roberts 2000 describes Mukulu as a pitch accent-type language whose verbs show a restricted set of tone patterns (culminative H / accent), with no statement of where the accent falls. Together with Lukas 1977 (phonology/Druckakzent explicitly not investigated; a future suffix noted as bearing Druckakzent and a falling tone, p. 199 snippet) and Jungraithmayr 1990 (two-tone system, no accent section), the evidence supports coding Mukulu as a tone/pitch accent language rather than a fixed-stress language; the placement rule (if any) is only in the unobtained Roberts 2000.

tone_statements.quote: Chadic languages are tonal. Many Chadic languages (e.g. Migaama, Mofu and Mukulu) are open to analysis as 'accentual languages' in which there is at most one H tone per word which is accompanied by other indicators of prominence (Pearce 2006), but others (e.g. Kera, Masa and Podoko) have three tones and a variety of lexical tone melodies on nouns.

sources.note: p. 19-20 'Les tons': two level tones, haut (á) and bas (à), combining into falling (â) and rising (ǎ) contours, with minimal pairs/triplets (bèerè 'choisir' : bèeré 'enquête' : béerè 'arbre sp.'); falling tone only word-medial except loans/ideophones; secondary falling tone from H + low definite suffix -n (kùlé-n > kùlên). In-volume searches for 'accent', "l'accent", 'accentué(e)', 'accentuation', 'intensité', 'intonation', 'prosodie' return zero hits: no statement on stress/accent detectable.
